title: The Three Visits in Reverse? One Volume, Two Versions: Zhuge Liang Came to Liu Bei
description:
You've surely heard of the three visits to the thatched cottage: Liu Bei went three times before Zhuge Liang agreed to come. But in the same volume of the Records of the Three Kingdoms that records it, Pei Songzhi's notes copy another version: Zhuge Liang went north to Fancheng on his own and stayed behind after a gathering broke up, while Liu Bei sat braiding a bundle of yak tail.

This episode goes through the original text. Chen Shou's main text, the Biography of Zhuge Liang, says that while Liu Bei was stationed at Xinye, Xu Shu recommended "Zhuge Kongming is a sleeping dragon"; Liu Bei told him, "Come with him"; Xu Shu said, "This man can be visited, but not summoned"; and so "the Former Lord went to Liang; three trips, then he saw him." The wasted first trip, the snowstorm, the nap and Zhang Fei threatening to set a fire are plot from chapters 37 and 38 of the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Pei Songzhi's notes quote the Weilüe: "Bei and Liang were not old friends"; "General, you should aim higher. Is braiding yak-tail ornaments all you do?"; "Your men number only a few thousand"; and the unregistered households are to "register themselves". He adds that the Jiuzhou Chunqiu "says the same". Then, after "Your servant Songzhi believes", he quotes Zhuge Liang's Chushi Biao (Memorial on Dispatching the Troops), "Not deeming me lowly, the late emperor stooped to visit me three times in my thatched cottage", rules "Clearly, then, Liang did not go to Bei first", and adds that for the two accounts to clash this much "is truly strange".

Boundaries: that the two meetings can't be put in order is this episode's own test of the possibilities, not Pei Songzhi's reasoning. Whose account the Weilüe's story first came from, and whether it and the Jiuzhou Chunqiu drew on separate sources, the notes don't say, so this page stays "open". The date of around 207 AD is Pei Songzhi's calculation from the number of years given in the Chushi Biao.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone; scrolls and memorials are drawn without writing, and the original text appears on text cards.

Information as of 2026-10-19 (rewritten under new rules on 2026-10-25)

chapters.pingren: They meet; Guan Yu, Zhang Fei sulk
chapters.weilue: Zhuge Liang goes north to Fancheng

gm101.text: You know the three visits: Liu Bei went three times to win Zhuge Liang.

gm102.text: But the same volume of history that records it copies another version, the exact reverse.

gm103.text: Fancheng. A gathering at Liu Bei's has just broken up. The guests are gone; only one young man stays behind.

gm104.text: Liu Bei doesn't ask what he wants. He looks down, braiding yak tail just sent to him.

gm105.text: This young man who won't leave is Zhuge Liang.

gm106.text: No one invited him. What did he stay to say?

gm107.text: Odder still, Pei Songzhi, who annotated this volume, copied it in, then added a passage of his own.

gm108.text: This file goes through that volume to see how two first meetings, facing opposite ways, ended up in one book.

gm109.text: So: did Liu Bei make three visits, or did Zhuge Liang come to his door?

gm201.text: The version where Liu Bei goes to him is in this volume's main text, by Chen Shou.

gm202.text: It starts in Xinye, where Liu Bei was stationed. A man named Xu Shu came to see him; Liu Bei valued him.

gm203.text: Xu Shu recommended someone: "Zhuge Kongming is a sleeping dragon."

gm204.text: This Jingzhou farmer likened himself to Guan Zhong and Yue Yi.

gm205.text: Hear a friend say that and you'd likely roll your eyes.

gm206.text: But Chen Shou says the friends who believed he really had that talent were Cui Zhouping and Xu Shu.

gm207.text: So what was Liu Bei's first reaction?

gm208.text: He said: "Come with him." Bring him along.

gm209.text: I think that's fair: the boss wants him, so send for him.

gm210.text: But Xu Shu said: "This man can be visited, but not summoned."

gm211.text: Meaning you must go to him; he can't be made to come.

gm212.text: He added: "You, General, should stoop to call on him." Go see him in person.

gm213.text: Would a general with troops go out in person for a country farmer?

gm214.text: Chen Shou: "So the Former Lord went to Liang: three trips, then he saw him."

gm215.text: The Former Lord is Liu Bei. He went himself three times before they met.

gm216.text: So where do the empty first trip and snowy second you recall come from?

gm217.text: That's the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms; on its third trip, Liu Bei waits outside as Zhuge Liang naps.

gm218.text: Chen Shou's main text has none of this. Which day each trip was, which road: he doesn't write a word.

gm219.text: Honestly, I was a bit let down at first: history gives the three trips five characters.

gm220.text: Once they met, Liu Bei sent others away and asked one thing. What was it?

gm301.text: The times first: the Han is in decline.

gm302.text: Then himself: "my wits are shallow"; he lacks plans.

gm303.text: Finally: "What's the plan?" What should he do next?

gm304.text: Saying you're not smart enough at a first meeting? Reading this, I quite admire him.

gm305.text: Zhuge Liang's answer was long. In short: don't fight Cao Cao head-on; Sun Quan can be an ally, Jingzhou and Yizhou a base.

gm306.text: At the time, Liu Bei held neither Jingzhou nor Yizhou; this was a plan, not a conquest.

gm307.text: You're Liu Bei. After all that, what do you say?

gm308.text: Liu Bei replied with one word: "Good." From then on, they "grew closer by the day."

gm309.text: So close that people beside them got upset: Guan Yu and Zhang Fei.

gm310.text: In the novel, Zhang Fei yells at the door to torch the back; Guan Yu stops him. Not in Chen Shou either.

gm311.text: In Chen Shou, they're upset only after the meeting. How did Liu Bei answer?

gm312.text: "I have Kongming as a fish has water." To me, he's like water to a fish.

gm313.text: With that, they dropped it. Remember this fish and water; soon it'll trip something up.

gm314.text: That's Chen Shou's version. And the other one Pei Songzhi copied beneath this passage: which book is it from?

gm401.text: Pei Songzhi traces the opening's reversed version to a book: the Weilüe.

gm402.text: Chen Shou didn't revise it; Pei Songzhi copied another book beside it.

gm403.text: The Weilüe: Liu Bei was at Fancheng; Cao Cao had just taken the north.

gm404.text: Zhuge Liang thought Cao Cao might push on Jingzhou next, and slow Liu Biao likely couldn't hold.

gm405.text: So he went north to Fancheng to see Liu Bei; in this passage, Xu Shu doesn't appear.

gm406.text: You're Liu Bei, and a young stranger shows up. How would you receive him?

gm407.text: The Weilüe: "Bei and Liang were not old friends." They'd never met.

gm408.text: Seeing his youth, Liu Bei treated him as a mere student. That gap threw me on first read too.

gm409.text: Remember the opening's gathering and the yak tail? That's when Zhuge Liang spoke.

gm410.text: General, you should aim higher. Is braiding yak-tail ornaments all you do?

gm411.text: Honestly, that's a bit rude to say to a general.

gm412.text: Sensing a rare man, Liu Bei threw down the tail:

gm413.text: "What talk is this? I only do it to forget my cares." It's just a way to unwind.

gm414.text: Caught twirling a pen in a dull meeting by the new guy? Probably that same look.

gm415.text: Pastime or not, this guest is about to run the numbers for Liu Bei. What numbers?

gm501.text: Headcount. First he asks: Liu Biao against Cao Cao, who's stronger? Liu Bei: no match.

gm502.text: Then: and you yourself, General? Again Liu Bei says: no match.

gm503.text: Zhuge Liang, plainly: "Your men number only a few thousand."

gm504.text: A few thousand against Cao Cao? You'd probably sweat for him too.

gm505.text: Liu Bei didn't argue: "I worry about it too. What can be done?"

gm506.text: Zhuge Liang says Jingzhou doesn't lack people; too few are on the registers.

gm509.text: His plan: tell Liu Biao to let Jingzhou's unregistered households register, then add men from the rolls.

gm510.text: Put simply, a census. The first move toward an empire is a census? Not romantic in the least.

gm512.text: The Weilüe doesn't say. Only: Liu Bei followed it, and his army grew strong.

gm513.text: Liu Bei now saw the young man was a gifted strategist;

gm514.text: and upgraded him to honored guest.

gm515.text: Pei Songzhi adds a line after this: another book, the Jiuzhou Chunqiu, says the same.

gm516.text: Two books say so. Sounds more believable now, right?

gm517.text: So one meeting is at the cottage, one at Fancheng. Could both have happened, one after the other?

gm602.text: Remember the fish and the water? In this order, Liu Bei already sees him as his water.

gm603.text: So at Fancheng, "Bei and Liang were not old friends" breaks: how could a fish not know water?

gm604.text: And the other way round, Fancheng first?

gm605.text: Then by Xinye, Zhuge Liang is already Liu Bei's honored guest.

gm606.text: But by Chen Shou's account, Xu Shu, recommending him, also asked Liu Bei: "General, would you be willing to see him?"

gm607.text: Already an honored guest, yet a friend asks "will you see him?" That fails too.

gm608.text: There's one more way: say one of them was a reunion. Does that work?

gm609.text: Chen Shou never calls the trips a reunion after Fancheng; the Weilüe never says they met before.

gm610.text: Neither passage has a date; nothing at all to order them by.

gm611.text: See: whatever the order, you'd have to add a line the ancients didn't write. That line I won't write for them.

gm612.text: What yardstick did Pei Songzhi, who set them side by side, use back then?

gm701.text: His yardstick was a memorial Zhuge Liang wrote himself: the Chushi Biao.

gm702.text: After the Jiuzhou Chunqiu line, he first writes "Your servant Songzhi believes"; from there, the words are his.

gm703.text: In 227, about to march north, Zhuge Liang wrote this memorial before setting out, for Liu Bei's son Liu Shan.

gm704.text: Liu Bei had died; Zhuge Liang tells the young emperor how he met the late emperor.

gm705.text: Of himself: "I was a commoner, farming in Nanyang," seeking no fame among lords.

gm706.text: And their meeting? How does he tell it?

gm707.text: "Not deeming me lowly, the late emperor stooped to visit me three times in my thatched cottage."

gm708.text: Beibi, "despicable" today, here means humble birth, not an insult. On a CV, footnote it.

gm709.text: Weizi wangqu means stooping to visit. So who in this line is stooping?

gm710.text: The late emperor is Liu Bei; "me" is Zhuge Liang. Liu Bei stooped to walk to the cottage.

gm711.text: Next: "he asked me of current affairs." Remember the cottage's "What's the plan?"

gm712.text: The memorial, too: first the visit, then the questions.

gm713.text: Then: "Moved by this, I promised the late emperor to toil for him." He agreed to serve Liu Bei.

gm714.text: By this memorial, he says, it had been "twenty-one years." Of course, that's memory, not a diary entry.

gm715.text: In another note, Pei Songzhi counts back from it:

gm716.text: They first met the year before Liu Bei's army was routed, around 207 AD.

gm717.text: Pei Songzhi's verdict on the Weilüe?

gm718.text: "Clearly, then, Liang did not go to Bei first." It wasn't Zhuge Liang who went first.

gm719.text: Pei Songzhi admits people hear and see differently, so accounts naturally differ. But that's not his last word.

gm720.text: Remember the passage he added after copying it? Its last two characters are keguai: to clash this much is truly strange.

gm721.text: I find that remarkable: he thought it strange, yet still copied it for later readers.

gm722.text: So who first told this strange version?

gm801.text: The Weilüe's Fancheng story doesn't say who told it.

gm802.text: Pei Songzhi marked it "the Weilüe says"; all we can know is which book he copied from.

gm803.text: And the Jiuzhou Chunqiu? It agrees with the Weilüe. Is that a second source?

gm804.text: Pei Songzhi wrote five characters: "it says the same." Its own words he didn't copy.

gm805.text: So we can't match the two books' details line by line.

gm806.text: Separate sources or one shared source? The note doesn't say.

gm807.text: Here the trail ends. Like me, you're probably a bit frustrated.

gm809.text: Chen Shou's preface to the Zhuge Liang Ji also says "three visits to Liang in his cottage."

gm810.text: But that's Chen Shou again: one author isn't two witnesses.

gm811.text: This side has a participant's own words: the Chushi Biao.

gm812.text: So, this file: Liu Bei calling on Zhuge Liang, archived. Who started the tale of Zhuge Liang calling first: open.

gm813.text: You're Pei Songzhi: keep it in the notes, or cut it? Tell me below.

gm814.text: This channel sticks to the record. Open files with us: subscribe.
